text:
A gas is kept in a container having walls which are thermally non-conducting. Initially the gas has a volume of $800\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ and temperature $27^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$. The change in temperature when the gas is adiabatically compressed to $200\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ is:

(Take $γ=1.5;γ$ is the ratio of specific heats at constant pressure and at constant volume)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the change in temperature when a gas is adiabatically compressed, we are given the following initial conditions:

Initial volume, $V_{1}=800\text{cm}^{3}$

Final volume, $V_{2}=200\text{cm}^{3}$

Initial temperature, $T_{1}=27^{\circ }\text{C}=300\text{K}$

Adiabatic index (ratio of specific heats) $γ=1.5$

In an adiabatic process, the relationship between temperature and volume is given by the equation:

$TV^{γ-1}=\text{constant}$

Applying this to the initial and final states:

$300\times (800)^{0.5}=T_{2}\times (200)^{0.5}$

Solving for the final temperature $T_{2}$:

$T_{2}=300\times \left (\frac{800}{200}\right )^{0.5}=300\times (4)^{0.5}$

$T_{2}=300\times 2=600\text{K}$

Thus, the change in temperature is:

$\Delta T=T_{2}-T_{1}=600\text{K}-300\text{K}=300\text{K}$

Therefore, when the gas is adiabatically compressed, the temperature increases by 300 K.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text: A wire of length 25 m and cross-sectional area $5\mathrm{mm}^{2}$ having resistivity of $2\times 10^{-6}\Omega \mathrm{m}$ is bent into a complete circle. The resistance between diametrically opposite points will be
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
[IMG]


Length of the wire, $L=25\mathrm{m}$  

Cross‐sectional area, $A=5\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}^{2}=5\times 10^{-6}\mathrm{m}^{2}$  

Resistivity, $ρ=2\times 10^{-6}\Omega \cdot m$  

Resistance of the entire wire:  

$R_{\mathrm{t}\mathrm{o}\mathrm{t}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{l}}=\frac{ρL}{A}=\frac{2\times 10^{-6}\times 25}{5\times 10^{-6}}=\frac{50\times 10^{-6}}{5\times 10^{-6}}=10\Omega$

When bent into a circle, points diametrically opposite divide the ring into two equal halves.  

Each half-circle has length $L/2=12.5\mathrm{m}$, so its resistance is half of $R_{\mathrm{t}\mathrm{o}\mathrm{t}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{l}}$:  

$R_{\mathrm{h}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{l}\mathrm{f}}=\frac{R_{\mathrm{t}\mathrm{o}\mathrm{t}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{l}}}{2}=\frac{10}{2}=5\Omega$

These two $5~\Omega$ halves are in parallel between the opposite points.  

Equivalent resistance $R$ is given by:  

$\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{h}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{l}\mathrm{f}}}+\frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{h}\mathrm{a}\mathrm{l}\mathrm{f}}}=\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{5}=\frac{2}{5}$  

$R=\frac{5}{2}=2.5\Omega$

Answer: 2.5 Ω (Option B)

text: The work function of a metal is 3 eV . The color of the visible light that is required to cause emission of photoelectrons is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine which color of visible light will cause the emission of photoelectrons from a metal with a work function of 3 eV, we need to consider the relationship between the photon energy, the work function, and the wavelength of light.

The maximum kinetic energy ($\text{KE}_{\max }$) of the emitted photoelectrons is given by:

$\text{KE}_{\max }=\frac{hc}{λ}-𝜙$

For photoemission to occur, the energy of the incident photons must be greater than the work function ($𝜙$):

$\frac{hc}{λ}>𝜙$

This implies:

$λ<\frac{hc}{𝜙}$

Substitute the values $h=4.135667696\times 10^{-15}\text{eV}\cdot \text{s}$, $c=3\times 10^{8}\text{m/s}$, and $𝜙=3\text{eV}$:

$λ<\frac{1242}{3}\text{nm}\approx 414\text{nm}$

Since the wavelength must be less than 414 nm to cause emission, we need light with a shorter wavelength. Among the visible colors, blue light has a wavelength in this range, making it the correct choice. Thus, blue light will cause the emission of photoelectrons with this work function.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Here’s how each quantity lines up with its dimensional formula:

Gravitational constant, $G$  

• From Newton’s law $F=G\frac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}$  

• $[G]=\frac{[F][r]^{2}}{[m]^{2}}=\frac{(MLT^{-2})L^{2}}{M^{2}}=M^{-1}L^{3}T^{-2}$  

⇒ IV

Gravitational potential energy, $U$  

• As work or $U=mgh$  

• $[U]=[F][h]=(MLT^{-2})L=ML^{2}T^{-2}$  

⇒ III

Gravitational potential, $𝜙$  

• Energy per unit mass: $𝜙=\frac{U}{m}$  

• $[𝜙]=\frac{ML^{2}T^{-2}}{M}=L^{2}T^{-2}$  

⇒ II

Acceleration due to gravity, $g$  

• Just an acceleration  

• $[g]=LT^{-2}$  

⇒ I

Matching them gives  

A–IV, B–III, C–II, D–I  

That corresponds to Option A.

text:
Consider a completely full cylindrical water tank of height 1.6 m and of cross-sectional area $0.5\mathrm{m}^{2}$. It has a small hole in its side at a height 90 cm from the bottom. Assume, the cross-sectional area of the hole to be negligibly small as compared to that of the water tank. If a load 50 kg is applied at the top surface of the water in the tank then the velocity of the water coming out at the instant when the hole is opened is:

$\left (\mathrm{g}=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}\right )$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The hole is $1.6-0.9=0.7\text{m}$ below the top surface. The load adds a pressure on the top surface:

$\dfrac{mg}{A}=\dfrac{50\times 10}{0.5}=1000\text{Pa}$


[IMG]

Point 1 is on the top surface and point 2 at the hole; both are open to the atmospheric pressure $P_{0}$. The hole is negligibly small compared with the tank, so the top surface is practically at rest, $v_{1}\approx 0$.

Bernoulli's equation between 1 and 2, with $ρ=10^{3}\text{kg m}^{-3}$ for water:

$P_{0}+\dfrac{mg}{A}+ρgh=P_{0}+\dfrac{1}{2}ρv^{2}$

$1000+10^{3}\times 10\times 0.7=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 10^{3}v^{2}$

$8000=500v^{2}\Rightarrow v^{2}=16\Rightarrow v=4\text{m s}^{-1}$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

text:
Consider following statements for refraction of light through prism, when angle of deviation is minimum.

A. The refracted ray inside prism becomes parallel to the base.

B. Larger angle prisms provide smaller angle of minimum deviation.

C. Angle of incidence and angle of emergence becomes equal.

D. There are always two sets of angle of incidence for which deviation will be same except at minimum deviation setting.

E. Angle of refraction becomes double of prism angle.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically through the prism: $i=e$ and $r_{1}=r_{2}=r$.

Statement A is true: with $r_{1}=r_{2}$ the ray inside makes equal angles with both refracting faces, so it runs parallel to the base.

Statement C is true: $i=e$ at minimum deviation.

Statement D is true: by reversibility of light, incidence at $i$ and at $e$ produce the same deviation, so every deviation other than $δ_{\min }$ is obtained for two angles of incidence; only at $δ_{\min }$ do the two coincide ($i=e$).

Statement B is false: $μ=\dfrac{\sin \left (\frac{A+δ_{\min }}{2}\right )}{\sin \left (\frac{A}{2}\right )}$ (for a thin prism $δ_{\min }=(μ-1)A$), so $δ_{\min }$ increases with the prism angle $A$.

Statement E is false: $r_{1}+r_{2}=A$ with $r_{1}=r_{2}$ gives $r=\dfrac{A}{2}$, half the prism angle.

The correct statements are A, C and D.

Hence, the correct option is (D).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

solution.body:
[IMG]


Area of plate is A. then

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{C}=\dfrac{ε_{2}ε_{0}\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{d}/2}=\dfrac{2ε_{2}ε_{0}\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{d}} \\ \mathrm{C}^{'}=\dfrac{ε_{1}ε_{0}\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{d}/2}=\dfrac{2ε_{1}ε_{0}\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{d}} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \text{Let}\mathrm{C}_{0}=\dfrac{ε_{0}\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{d}} \\ \mathrm{C}=2ε_{2}\mathrm{C}_{0} \\ \mathrm{C}^{'}=2ε_{1}\mathrm{C}_{0} \end{array}$

C & C' are in series

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{C}_{1}=\dfrac{\mathrm{CC}^{'}}{\mathrm{C}+\mathrm{C}^{'}}=\dfrac{4ε_{2}ε_{1}\mathrm{C}_{0}^{2}}{2\mathrm{C}_{0}(ε_{2}+ε_{1})} \\ =\dfrac{2ε_{2}ε_{1}\mathrm{C}_{0}}{(ε_{2}+ε_{1})} \end{array}$


[IMG]


Here $C=\frac{ε_{1}ε_{0}A}{2d}=\frac{ε_{1}C_{0}}{2}$

$C^{'}=\frac{ε_{2}C_{0}}{2}$

$\mathrm{C}&\mathrm{C}^{'}$ are in parallel

$\mathrm{C}_{2}=\mathrm{C}^{'}+\mathrm{C}=(ε_{1}+ε_{2})\frac{\mathrm{C}_{0}}{2}$

Thus $\frac{\mathrm{C}_{1}}{\mathrm{C}_{2}}=\frac{2ε_{2}ε_{1}\mathrm{C}_{0}}{(ε_{2}+ε_{1})}\times \frac{2}{(ε_{1}+ε_{2})\mathrm{C}_{0}}$

$=\frac{4ε_{2}ε_{1}}{(ε_{2}+ε_{1})^{2}}$

text: During the melting of a slab of ice at 273 K at atmospheric pressure :
options: Internal energy of ice-water system remains unchanged.
Positive work is done by the ice-water system on the atmosphere.
Positive work is done on the ice-water system by the atmosphere.
Internal energy of the ice-water system decreases.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Water at 273 K is denser than ice, so the volume of the ice-water system decreases as the slab melts ($\Delta V<0$) while the pressure stays at the atmospheric value $P_{0}$.

The work done by the system is $W=P_{0}\Delta V<0$; equivalently, the atmosphere does positive work $P_{0}\quad |\Delta V|$ on the ice-water system.

The system absorbs latent heat, $Q=mL>0$. By the first law, with $W$ the work done by the system,

$\Delta U=Q-W=mL+P_{0}|\Delta V|>0$

So the internal energy increases even though the temperature stays at 273 K, which rules out (A) and (D); (B) reverses the sign of the work.

Hence, the correct option is (C).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text: A particle is released from height $S$ above the surface of the earth. At certain height its kinetic energy is three times its potential energy. The height from the surface of the earth and the speed of the particle at that instant are respectively.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Using the equation of motion for velocity at height $x$:  

$V^{2}=0+2g(S-x)$

Simplifies to:

$V^{2}=2g(S-x)$

Potential Energy at height $x$:  

$\text{Potential Energy}=mgx$

Relation between kinetic and potential energy:  

Given that the kinetic energy is three times the potential energy,

$\frac{1}{2}mV^{2}=3\times mgx$

Simplifying gives:

$\frac{1}{2}\times 2g(S-x)=3gx$

$g(S-x)=3gx$

$4x=S$

Solving for $x$:

$x=\frac{S}{4}$

Finding the speed $V$ at this instant:

$V=\sqrt{2g\left (S-\frac{S}{4}\right )}=\sqrt{2g\times \frac{3S}{4}}=\sqrt{\frac{3gS}{2}}$

Thus, the height from the surface of the Earth is $\frac{S}{4}$ and the speed of the particle at that height is $\sqrt{\frac{3gS}{2}}$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

solution.body:
$\begin{array}{l} \text{(A) As both blocks moving together so} \\ \begin{array}{l} \text{Time period}=2π\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{K}}};\text{where}\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{M}+\mathrm{m} \\ \mathrm{T}=2π\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{M}+\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{K}}} \end{array} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} KA=(M+m)a \\ a=\dfrac{KA}{(M+m)} \\ f=ma=\dfrac{mKA}{(M+m)} \\ f_{\max }=f_{L}=μmg \\ f=μmg \\ \dfrac{mKA}{(M+m)}=μmg \\ A=\dfrac{μ(M+m)g}{K} \end{array}$

text: The radii of curvature for a thin convex lens are 10 cm and 15 cm respectively. The focal length of the lens is 12 cm . The refractive index of the lens material is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the refractive index ($μ$) of a thin convex lens, we use the lens maker's formula:

$\frac{1}{f}=(μ-1)\left (\frac{1}{R_{1}}-\frac{1}{R_{2}}\right )$

Given:

Focal length ($f$) = 12 cm

Radii of curvature ($R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$) = 10 cm and -15 cm, respectively

Substituting these values into the formula, we have:

$\frac{1}{12}=(μ-1)\left (\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{-15}\right )$

Simplifying the equation:

$\frac{1}{12}=(μ-1)\left (\frac{3+2}{30}\right )$

$\frac{1}{12}=(μ-1)\times \frac{5}{30}$

$\frac{1}{12}=(μ-1)\times \frac{1}{6}$

Solving for $μ$:

$μ-1=\frac{1}{12}\times 6$

$μ-1=\frac{1}{2}$

$μ=\frac{3}{2}$

Thus, the refractive index of the lens material is $μ=1.5$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text: The electrostatic potential on the surface of uniformly charged spherical shell of radius $\mathrm{R}=10\mathrm{cm}$ is 120 V . The potential at the centre of shell, at a distance $\mathrm{r}=5\mathrm{cm}$ from centre, and at a distance $\mathrm{r}=15$ cm from the centre of the shell respectively, are:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The potential inside a uniformly charged spherical shell is equal to the potential on its surface. This means:

$V_{\text{in}}=V_{\text{surface}}=\frac{kQ}{R}=120\text{V}$

This maintains the potential at both the center of the shell and any point inside it up to the surface. Therefore, the potential at the center of the shell and at any point inside the shell (like at a distance $r=5\text{cm}$) is also $120\text{V}$.

For a point outside the shell, at a distance $r=15\text{cm}$, the potential is given by the formula:

$V=\frac{kQ}{r}=\frac{120\times 10}{15}=80\text{V}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text: The radiation pressure exerted by a 450 W light source on a perfectly reflecting surface placed at 2 m away from it, is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
First, the intensity $I$ at a distance $r$ from a point light source spreading its energy isotropically is given by  

$I=\frac{P}{4πr^{2}},$  

where  

$P=450\text{W}$  

$r=2\text{m}.$  

So,  

$I=\frac{450}{4π(2)^{2}}=\frac{450}{16π}\approx \frac{450}{50.27}\approx 8.96\text{W/m}^{2}.$

For a perfectly reflecting surface, the radiation pressure $p$ is given by  

$p=\frac{2I}{c},$  

where $c\approx 3\times 10^{8}\text{m/s}$ is the speed of light.

Substituting the value of $I$:  

$p=\frac{2\times 8.96}{3\times 10^{8}}\approx \frac{17.92}{3\times 10^{8}}\text{Pa}.$

Calculating the final value:  

$p\approx 5.97\times 10^{-8}\text{Pa},$  

which is approximately $6\times 10^{-8}\text{Pa}.$

Thus, the correct answer is:

Option D: $6\times 10^{-8}$ Pascals.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text:
In the figure shown below, a resistance of $150.4\Omega$ is connected in series to an ammeter A of resistance $240\Omega$. A shunt resistance of $10\Omega$ is connected in parallel with the ammeter. The reading of the ammeter $is___________mA$ .

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
[IMG]


Step 1: Find the Total Resistance

First, add up the resistor in series ($R_{1}=150.4\Omega$) with the combined resistance of the ammeter and its shunt ($R_{2}$).

The ammeter ($240\Omega$) is in parallel with a shunt of ($10\Omega$). The combined resistance of resistors in parallel is found by:

$R_{2}=\frac{240\times 10}{240+10}=\frac{2400}{250}=9.6\Omega$

The total resistance ($R_{eq}$) is:

$R_{eq}=150.4+9.6=160\Omega$

Step 2: Find the Current in the Circuit

Suppose the total current in the circuit is $I$. But to find the ammeter reading, we care about the current through the ammeter coil itself.

The current through the ammeter, $I_{1}$, is given by how the current splits between the ammeter and the shunt. The fraction going through the ammeter is:

$I_{1}=\frac{R_{2}}{240}\times I$

But $R_{2}=9.6\Omega$ (the parallel combination), and $240\Omega$ is the ammeter's resistance:

$I_{1}=\frac{9.6}{240}\times I$

Step 3: Substitute the Circuit Values

The supply voltage is $20V$. The total resistance is $160\Omega$. So the total current is:

$I=\frac{20}{160}=0.125A$

So:

$I_{1}=0.125\times \frac{9.6}{240}$

Calculate this:

$I_{1}=0.125\times 0.04=0.005A=5\text{mA}$

Final Answer:

The ammeter reads $5\text{mA}$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text:
A loop ABCDA , carrying current $\mathrm{I}=12\mathrm{A}$, is placed in a plane, consists of two semi-circular segments of radius $R_{1}=6π\mathrm{m}$ and $\mathrm{R}_{2}=4π\mathrm{m}$. The magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at center O is $\mathrm{k}\times 10^{-7}\mathrm{T}$. The value of $k is_________$.

( Given $μ_{0}=4π\times 10^{-7}\mathrm{Tm}\mathrm{A}^{-1}$ )

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Magnetic Field from Semi-Circular Segments:

The magnetic field at the center due to a semi-circular loop is given by:

$B=\frac{μ_{0}I}{4R}$

Calculating $B_{R_{1}}$ and $B_{R_{2}}$:

For the semi-circle with radius $R_{1}$:

$B_{R_{1}}=\frac{μ_{0}I}{4R_{1}}=\frac{4π\times 10^{-7}\times 12}{4\times 6π}$

For the semi-circle with radius $R_{2}$:

$B_{R_{2}}=\frac{μ_{0}I}{4R_{2}}=\frac{4π\times 10^{-7}\times 12}{4\times 4π}$

Net Magnetic Field at the Center (O):

The total magnetic field $B_{0}$ at the center is the difference between these two fields (since they are in opposite directions):

$B_{0}=|B_{R_{1}}-B_{R_{2}}|$

Calculate:

$B_{0}=\frac{4π\times 10^{-7}\times 12}{4}\left (\frac{1}{4π}-\frac{1}{6π}\right )$

$B_{0}=12π\times 10^{-7}\left (\frac{1}{12π}\right )$

$B_{0}=1\times 10^{-7}\text{T}$

Value of $k$:

Given that the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field is $k\times 10^{-7}\text{T}$, we find $k=1$.

Thus, the value of $k$ is 1.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text: Two coherent monochromatic light beams of intensities 4I and 9I are superimposed. The difference between the maximum and minimum intensities in the resulting interference pattern is $x\mathrm{I}$. The value of $x$ $is___________$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Calculate Maximum Intensity ($I_{\text{\max }}$):

$I_{\max }=\left (\sqrt{I_{1}}+\sqrt{I_{2}}\right )^{2}$

Substituting the values, we have:

$I_{\max }=\left (\sqrt{4I}+\sqrt{9I}\right )^{2}$

$I_{\max }=\left (2\sqrt{I}+3\sqrt{I}\right )^{2}=\left (5\sqrt{I}\right )^{2}=25I$

Calculate Minimum Intensity ($I_{\text{\min }}$):

$I_{\min }=\left (\sqrt{I_{1}}-\sqrt{I_{2}}\right )^{2}$

Substituting the values, we have:

$I_{\min }=\left (\sqrt{4I}-\sqrt{9I}\right )^{2}$

$I_{\min }=\left (2\sqrt{I}-3\sqrt{I}\right )^{2}=\left (-1\sqrt{I}\right )^{2}=I$

Calculate the Difference Between Maximum and Minimum Intensities:

$I_{\max }-I_{\min }=25I-I=24I$

Thus, the value of $x$, which represents the difference between the maximum and minimum intensities, is $24$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text: Three identical spheres of mass m , are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of length $a$. When released, they interact only through gravitational force and collide after a time $\mathrm{T}=4$ seconds. If the sides of the triangle are increased to length $2a$ and also the masses of the spheres are made 2 m , then they will collide after$__________$seconds.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Released from rest in the same equilateral arrangement, the time $t$ to collide depends only on $G$, $m$ and $a$; the dimensionless shape factor is the same for both triangles. Let $t\propto G^{x}m^{y}a^{z}$ with $[G]=[\text{M}^{-1}\text{L}^{3}\text{T}^{-2}]$:

$[\text{M}^{0}\text{L}^{0}\text{T}^{1}]=[\text{M}^{-x+y}\text{L}^{3x+z}\text{T}^{-2x}]$

$-2x=1\Rightarrow x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$, then $y=x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $z=-3x=\dfrac{3}{2}$, so

$t\propto \sqrt{\dfrac{a^{3}}{Gm}}$

With side $2a$ and masses $2m$:

$\dfrac{t^{'}}{t}=\sqrt{\dfrac{(2a)^{3}/(2m)}{a^{3}/m}}=\sqrt{4}=2\Rightarrow t^{'}=2\times 4=8\text{s}$

Hence, the answer is 8.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text: A 4.0 cm long straight wire carrying a current of 8 A is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.15 T . The magnetic force on the wire is $________mN$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To calculate the magnetic force on a wire, we use the formula:

$\mathrm{F}=\mathrm{I}\ell \mathrm{B}$

Where:

$\mathrm{I}$ is the current in the wire (in amperes),

$\ell$ is the length of the wire (in meters),

$\mathrm{B}$ is the magnetic field strength (in teslas).

Given that:

The current $\mathrm{I}$ is 8 A,

The length of the wire $\ell$ is 4.0 cm, which is 0.04 m (since 1 cm = 0.01 m),

The magnetic field strength $\mathrm{B}$ is 0.15 T,

Substituting these values into the formula gives:

$\mathrm{F}=8\times 0.04\times 0.15$

Calculating this:

$\mathrm{F}=0.048\mathrm{N}$

To convert this to millinewtons (mN), recall that $1~\mathrm{N}=1000\mathrm{mN}$. Therefore:

$\mathrm{F}=48\mathrm{mN}$

Thus, the magnetic force on the wire is 48 mN.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift
